97agep:251: "The scarce resource becomes structured understanding of work: what an artifact means, how it changes, who has the right to change it, how changes propagate, what is consistent"—this is the article's core argument closest to a "moat definition." In the UI-centric era, a product's moat was user experience and interaction patterns; in the agent-native era, the moat becomes "who owns the structured representation layer of the artifact." Companies that own the structural layer can flexibly switch between multiple rendering views and multiple agent interaction modes, while companies that don't own it can only rely on existing UI exports. This means: data model design matters far more than UI design in 2026.

i7g05k:246: The article's deepest proposition: software categories (Slides, Spreadsheets, Documents, CRMs, etc.) are not natural laws but accidents of interface history. This analysis reveals the deep structure of the SaaS ecosystem: existing software products are designed around UI and human interaction patterns, bundling data models, rendering engines, permission systems, compliance features, etc., into single product boundaries. The restructuring force of the AI era lies in: this bundling is no longer necessary, because a structured data layer can simultaneously serve multiple rendering views and multiple agents, rather than being limited to a single human user interface.
